messages.subject: Re: differential test function
messages.body_plain:
Hi Balazs,

Guido is correct in the interpretation that the invariance of the person/item parameters makes this task a little more straightforward by way of equating. For instance, assuming that there is no response bias between the items you could first constrain all the item parameters to be equal across the groups, and then freely estimate the latent mean in one of your groups of interest to reflect that the items may be easier/harder (depending on the observed mean shift). And, if you're wondering about a type of significance approach you could perform likelihood-ratio type tests via the anova function. Something like the following would do it.

##########
library(mirt)

a <- matrix(abs(rnorm(15,1,.3)), ncol=1)
d <- matrix(rnorm(15,0,.7),ncol=1)
itemtype <- rep('2PL', nrow(a))
N <- 1000
dataset1 <- simdata(a, d, N, itemtype)

# test is easier for this group (have higher ability)
dataset2 <- simdata(a, d, N, itemtype, mu = .2)

dat <- rbind(dataset1, dataset2)
group <- c(rep('D1', N), rep('D2', N))

# not equated (intercept estimates absorb the different ability distribution)
mod_configural <- multipleGroup(dat, 1, group = group)
coef(mod_configural, simplify=TRUE)

# equating fixes this problem
mod_scalar <- multipleGroup(dat, 1, group = group,
                            invariance=c(colnames(dat), 'free_means'))
coef(mod_scalar, simplify=TRUE)

# equivalent fit (constrained model does not fit unusually worse)
anova(mod_configural, mod_scalar)

#########

Phil

messages.subject: Re: meaning of p-value in M2 statistics
messages.subject_clean: meaning of p-value in M2 statistics
messages.body_plain:
The null hypothesis for this test is that the data moments (proportions/means, bivariate-tables/covariances) were generated assuming that the fitted model is the true population generating model (e.g., in the case of M2* that the item means and covariance matrix perfectly match the model-implied mean/covariance structure). The interpretation is largely the same as one finds in structural equation models's GOF statistics based on the chi-squared discrepancy (and in fact, C2* is exactly the same). Hence, higher p-values indicate less surprising misfit to the data, while small p-values more surprising misfit (and therefore more likely that the model is misspecified somewhere, resulting in misfits in the moments.).

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Are results from MCEM and EM methods comparable?
messages.subject_clean: Are results from MCEM and EM methods comparable?
messages.body_plain:
Yes, they are comparable as they are just different methods to perform numerical integration on the same problem. No doubt bfactor() will be superior though as the dimension reduction technique really helps to keep the number of integrals to evaluate small (e.g., as low as 2). It's likely possible to add MCEM to the bfactor() function for MC integration of the general dimensions while the specific dimensions use a fixed quadrature set, but I have no looked into this too closely.

Phil

Hi Phil and Guido,
thanks for the help.

Especially thanks for the reprex. It made all the difference to me.
Just to make sure I understand it correctly, in your example Phil :

- anova(mod_configural, mod_scalar)  - shows that the assumption of having equal slopes but not equal intercepts in the model is NOT a bad assumption
- anova(mod_scalar, mod_scalar0) - shows that the assumption of having both equal slopes and intercepts in the model IS a bad assumption

So I ran the analysis and found a significant difference. But it is a very large model, with more than 1k items. Here is the anova result:

Is there a way to quantify this difference?
Is it possible, and would it make sense to e.g. correlate the estimated scores between the two models?

Thanks
Balázs

messages.body_plain:
On Sun, Dec 5, 2021 at 2:22 PM Balazs Klein <balazs...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Phil and Guido,
> thanks for the help.
>
> Especially thanks for the reprex. It made all the difference to me.
> Just to make sure I understand it correctly, in your example Phil :
>
> - anova(mod_configural, mod_scalar)  - shows that the assumption of having equal slopes but not equal intercepts in the model is NOT a bad assumption

This model comparison assumes invariance of all the item parameters (in this case, slopes and intercepts), but accounts for observed response differences as a function of different latent trait mean properties (e.g., in an aptitude test, one group is systematically more able than another). This is basically a check to evaluate if this highly constrained model still fits the data reasonably well, which sets the stage for further isolated tests like DIF or DRF.

> - anova(mod_scalar, mod_scalar0) - shows that the assumption of having both equal slopes and intercepts in the model IS a bad assumption

No, they have the same IRT parameter constraints. The test in this case is that the groups have the same latent trait mean (i.e., on average have the same ability), which is likely problematic if there were notable  and systematic differences in the intercepts in the mod_configural setup.

>
> So I ran the analysis and found a significant difference. But it is a very large model, with more than 1k items. Here is the anova result:
>       AIC    AICc   SABIC      HQ     BIC    logLik       X2   df   p
> 1 1358868 1359107 1371736 1365214 1379068 -677127.0      NaN  NaN NaN
> 2 1359551 1360557 1385275 1372238 1399932 -675163.5 3927.146 2305   0
>
> Is there a way to quantify this difference?

You're comparing competing models, so the information indices are generally helpful here.

> Is it possible, and would it make sense to e.g. correlate the estimated scores between the two models?

Unlikely, as that introduces a good deal of dependency effects.

Phil

Hi All

I am a novice when it comes to both R and Item response theory models. I am working with a set of polytomous situational items having SME reviewed key from 1 to 4 (4 being the most appropriate response). Not all the items are presented to my testtakers, but they receive a random subset of the items. There would be some overlapping items, but no anchor items. I want to standardize my item bank, I currently have 99 items, and I am hoping to retain about 40-50 good items. I have the following queries:

1.       Is Multidimensional GPCM model the correct model for this data? If not, please suggest the alternative model.

2.       When I run the command > mod1<-mirt(data,1,itemtype=”gpcm”) followed by the command for coef(mod1) I am unable to interpret the output. What is meant by the terms ak0, ak1, ak2,ak3,d0?

3.       I am not sure if my items are unidimensional or multidimensional, so I would try out different models while specifying different factor numbers and subsequently verifying model fit using anova(mod1,mod2) function. Is this the right approach?

4.       How do I remove certain problematic items, lets say the ones where there is poor factor loading, or a negative a parameter? (I need help with the R command here to remove a particular item from the data set and then rerun my analysis)

5.       Since a large amount of data is missing because of the test design, can I consider that as MCAR and ignore it?

Please help me solve these issues. Anticipating a positive response.

If so, can we access the number of iterations and final incremental change in theta values? Is there a way to specify the number of iterations or the incremental change within the function as well?

Thank you,
Ozge

messages.subject: Re: fscores number of iterations

Hi Ozge,

No, fscores() does not use the Newton-Raphson optimizer but instead uses the Nealder-Mead by default since the optimization for each score is very low dimensional. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: comparing mirt and catR scores
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to compare mirt and catR scores.
I have a feeling that while their Theta estimates are very similar their Sem estimates are very different. I get strange patterns though for both comparison, and can't figure out why.

library(mirt)
library(mirtCAT)
nitems <- 100
a1 <- rlnorm(nitems, .2,.2)
d <- rnorm(nitems)
mirt.pars <- data.frame(a1=a1, d=d)
mirt.mod <- generate.mirt_object(mirt.pars, '2PL')

itemtype <- rep('2PL', nrow(mirt.pars))
nperson <- 100

dat <- simdata(a1, d, nperson, itemtype)
mirt.scores<-fscores(mirt.mod,response.pattern = dat)

library(catR)
cat.pars<-as.data.frame(coef(mirt.mod , simplify = TRUE, IRTpars = TRUE)$items[,c('a','b')])
cat.pars$d<-1
cat.pars$c<-0
cat.pars=as.matrix(cat.pars)

cat.scores<-
  do.call(
    rbind, apply(dat, 1, function(x) {
      cF1=thetaEst(cat.pars, x)
      cSem=semTheta(cF1, cat.pars)
      data.frame(cF1=cF1, cSem=cSem)
    })
  )

all.scores<-cbind(mirt.scores,cat.scores)

plot(all.scores$F1, all.scores$cF1)
plot(all.scores$SE_F1, all.scores$cSem)

messages.subject: Re: comparing mirt and catR scores
messages.body_plain:
You're comparing mirt's EAP and the PSD estimates to catR's EAP and SE estimates, which won't be the same since the SE does not contain information about the prior. You might have meant to use catR::eapSem().

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Detecting aberrant responses using person fit statistics
messages.subject_clean: Detecting aberrant responses using person fit statistics
messages.body_plain:
Was just looking through previous discussions to see if there was anything on what mirt does when computing person fit, and whether it has the lz* generalization to polytomous items. Came across this thread. I think generalizations of lz* do exist, but I don't (yet) see an R package that can do them:
http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/s11336-015-9465-x

On Monday, March 18, 2019 at 8:06:50 a.m. UTC-4 rphilip....@gmail.com wrote:
> I also am not aware of the polytomous generalization to this statistic, though it could very well be that nobody has generalized it yet. The PerFit package contains a number of these person-fit type indices, so you might have some luck there.
>
> Regarding the paper, the approach these authors took is a pretty aggressive one, and reminds me a lot of fitting regression models after iteratively removing all cases that have even minimally large residuals. An alternative strategy, which doesn't require the standardized lz* versions of the statistic, is to apply a weight function to each response vector according to these person fit measures.
>
> E.g., compute the original model, obtain Zh for each case (or lz*), and obtain the weight w = 1/abs(Zh). Given this weight vector, pass the result to the survey.weight input to re-estimate the model to obtain a model that is less influenced by the originally contaminated observations. Under this approach, cases that are initially deemed unusual get progressively less weight in the final model. You could obviously repeat this process if you wanted to, but in the end it has the same effect (and in the limiting case where the w -> 0 in really unusual cases then this is equivalent to removing the observations entirely. Hence, the data removal approach is a limiting subset of this weighted approach). HTH.
>
> Phil
>
>
> On Wed, Mar 13, 2019 at 11:24 AM AM <mut...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Dear Phil,
> >
> > I've been reading a paper (DOI: 10.3102/1076998618825116) where authors propose an iterative procedure to detect aberrant responses in a sample of test takers. Just to summarize the important points, this is what the procedure looks like:
> >
> > 1. Estimate item parameters on the full sample
> > 2. Flag participants whose person-fit statistic is below the cutoff
> > 3. Estimate item parameters on the reduced sample (without flagged participants). Use those item parameters from the REDUCED sample to compute person parameters from the FULL sample
> > 4. Repeat 2 & 3 until the difference in the percentage of flagged participant in the current and previous iteration is less than 0.01
> >
> > Now, my question: the authors in the linked paper use a lz* statistic of person fit. I am wondering do you think it would be possible to use the Zh statistic from your package to follow the same procedure? Are you aware of any theoretical and/or mathematical reasons that would prevent this usage? As far as I know, the lz* statistic is used only for binary items and I am interested in detecting aberrant responses on Likert scales.
> >
> > --
> > You received this message because you are subscribed to the Google Groups "mirt-package" group.
> > To unsubscribe from this group and stop receiving emails from it, send an email to mirt-package...@googlegroups.com.

messages.subject: Re: fscores number of iterations
messages.body_plain:
For criteria that require iterative estimation Neldar-Mead is the only one used (I don't see any reason not to use this criteria, as even with 6 dimensions in your case the parameter space is very small). The only other approaches used are those based on numerical integration (e.g., EAP, EAPsum), in which case the QMC input could make a difference in higher dimensional settings. In your case, I'd be tempted just to use the MAP criteria rather than EAP estimates as the two should correlate very well. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: multipleGroup and Missing Data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil. I love your package and am using it for my dissertation. I asked a question on Github but then found this forum and thought it would be more appropriate. I know several past threads have asked about multiple groups and missing data, but didn't seem to provide an answer to my question.

I am wondering how multipleGroup handles missing data? Specifically, if some groups are not administered an item, I would assume multipleGroup drops those items from the group-level analysis. However, in running the code below, that group (D) has item parameters for items that were all NAs (items 5, 10, 15, and 20).

For context, I am re-estimating PISA data and for some countries, some items were not included. Additionally, I am doing this across cycles (I have cycle-by-country groups). Many items were not asked across cycles, meaning there will be many columns with complete NAs for certain cycle-by-country groups (e.g. 2006-USA, 2009-USA would have different complete columns).

```

library(mirt)
library(tidyverse) # simulate data ---- set.seed(1234) N <- 1000 # create covariates ---- X1 <- rnorm(N); X2 <- rnorm(N) Theta <- matrix(0.5 * X1 + -1 * X2 + rnorm(N, sd = 0.5)) # create items and response data ---- a <- matrix(1, 20); d <- matrix(rnorm(20)) dat <- simdata(a, d, 1000, itemtype = '2PL', Theta=Theta) # create groups ---- groups <- c(rep("A", 250),rep("B", 250),rep("C", 250),rep("D", 250)) # generate missing values in item data ---- # group A - 50 missing values dat_a <- dat %>% as.data.frame() %>% slice(1:250) for (i in 1:50) { dat_a[sample(nrow(dat_a),1),sample(ncol(dat_a),1)] <- NA } # group B - complete cases dat_b <- dat %>% as.data.frame() %>% slice(251:500) #group C - 100 missing values dat_c <- dat %>% as.data.frame() %>% slice(501:750) for (i in 1:100) { dat_c[sample(nrow(dat_c),1),sample(ncol(dat_c),1)] <- NA } # group d - 5 missing columns dat_d<- dat %>% as.data.frame() %>% slice(751:1000) %>% mutate_at(vars(5,10,15,20), ~NA) # combine data dat2 <- rbind(dat_a, dat_b, dat_c, dat_d) # model with missing item data mod0 <- multipleGroup(dat2, 1, group=groups,'2PL', invariance = c("slopes", "intercepts", "free_mean", "free_var")) summary(mod0)
```

Thank you!

messages.subject: Re: multipleGroup and Missing Data
messages.body_plain:
In isolation group D's parameters are not estimable, and the responses contribute no information about the parameters anyway. So, you may as well set them either a) as fixed at some arbitrary values and ignore them in the output (I'm less fond of that as it can be confusing, but certainly viable), or b) set them equal to some other parameters that are estimable to completely 'borrow strength' from other parameters that do have valid observations (which is what your code does via the invariance input). Make sense?

Phil

Thanks for your explanation. The `multipleGroup` function will not run with missing data unless invariance parameters are set. Is there any way to allow items with some missing data to borrow from other valid observations while ignoring items that are completely missing data?  My next step after item parameter estimation is to then use `fscores` to draw plausible values. I'm not sure if it is valid to have items with completely missing values contribute to plausible values. Though, I may not completely understand how the values are being drawn.

Ultimately, I am running multi group on cycle-by country (e.g. 2006-USA, 2006-AUS, 2009-USA. 2009-AUS, etc) for 5 cycles and want to make sure my approach is correct. I can get around this by just estimating trend items, but I lose a lot of countries and information in the process.

Thanks for your help!!
